reason: E1 shows that passivation film on Q235 has weaknesses and sheds locally, but does not address high-temperature transformation or cracking. E2 shows that at 20–60 °C, higher temperature produces more Fe2O3 and a better, thicker passive film, directly contradicting the premise that high temperature creates a brittle, defect-rich layer. The key premises about film cracking, chloride penetration, and pitting at 800 °C are unsupported by the cited evidence.
premises: Pre-passivated Q235 steel has a dense, uniform passivation film
At ~800 °C, this film transforms into brittle Fe2O3/Fe3O4 with microcracking
Thermal expansion mismatch and chloride attack create film defects and cracks
Cracks allow chloride ion penetration and initiate pitting corrosion
At room temperature, the film remains intact and corrosion is slow
